tagline: A foothill loop linking the Southtowns, craft workshops and Cattaraugus Creek
intro: Southeast of Buffalo, the Western New York Southtowns Scenic Byway links highways through the foothills of the Allegheny Mountains. US 219, NY 240 and NY 242 carry the route through those foothills. New York State DOT describes a 108-mile scenic loop, including an alternative route, with scenic, historical, natural, cultural and recreational themes. In the northern section, the state DOT identifies Chestnut Ridge, Sprague Brook and Knox Farm parks among the scenic attractions. The southern extension also includes Griffis Sculpture Park, where steel sculptures have been installed on 450 acres since the early 1960s.

The corridor grew when New York State legislation approved an extension through Ashford and Ellicottville to the southern Ellicottville town line. That expansion put Springville and Concord in the center of the byway and brought it into Cattaraugus County. The byway organization describes its purpose as stewardship of the region’s natural, scenic, cultural, historic and recreational resources.

Begin with Orchard Park and East Aurora, where the northern attractions include Orchard Park’s railroad depot and the Roycroft Campus. Continue south through Colden and Concord to Springville and Scoby Dam. Beyond Cattaraugus Creek, NY 240 leads through West Valley toward NY 242 and Ellicottville; US 219 forms the corridor’s western border in Cattaraugus County.

moments.title: Roycroft Campus
moments.text: A book without a publisher helped start Roycroft: Elbert Hubbard could not place Little Journeys, so he established his own private press. Influenced by William Morris, Hubbard founded the East Aurora community in 1895. His Arts and Crafts ideas drew printers, furniture makers, metalsmiths, leatherworkers and bookbinders into a community. By 1910, almost 500 people had gathered there. Fourteen original buildings remain near South Grove and Main Street, giving the craft community a physical presence beyond its books and furniture. The campus received National Historic Landmark status in 1986, recognizing this surviving art colony.

moments.title: Springville
moments.text: Springville’s former name, Fiddler’s Green, survives as the title of a mural in its post office. Victoria Hutson Huntley painted the work as part of the federal Treasury Department’s mural program. The post office itself dates to 1936–1937: a one-story brick building in the Colonial Revival style, topped by a square cupola. The village also turned an older building toward the arts: Springville Center for the Arts occupies the former Baptist church, built in 1869 with red brick, limestone trim and a square corner bell tower. The arts organization purchased the church in June 2007.

moments.title: Scoby Dam
moments.text: Cattaraugus Creek once supplied electricity here, at a hydroelectric complex built in 1925 to replace an earlier facility nearby. The plant and dam occupy the creek’s eastern bank outside Springville, between Ashford and Concord. Springville stopped generating power at the dam in 1998. Erie County then acquired the dam and surrounding land, managing it as a conservation park with few improvements or facilities. The byway organization identifies Scoby Dam as a trout-fishing stop. The complex entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1996, two years before Springville ended its power generation.
